stemMd:
Although the lime plaster of a fresco is porous enough to take in centuries of candle ______ the pigment bound into its surface survives almost untouched, which is why a restorer can lift the grime without lifting the picture.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanationMd:
The word that decides this question is the first one: *Although*. A subordinating conjunction makes the clause it introduces dependent, and a dependent clause cannot stand as a sentence.

Test it out loud: "Although the lime plaster of a fresco is porous enough to take in centuries of candle smoke." That is a fragment — it leaves you waiting. So the punctuation at the blank must *join* this clause to the main clause that follows, not separate two sentences. When a dependent clause comes first, a comma does that job. Choice A.

Three of the marks on offer — semicolon, full stop, colon — all require a complete clause on their left, and there is none, so all three fail for the same reason. Naming that shared requirement is faster than testing each mark separately.

Check by flipping the clause order: "The pigment bound into its surface survives almost untouched although the lime plaster is porous enough to take in centuries of candle smoke." The sentence still works with no punctuation at the join, which confirms the two clauses belong to one sentence rather than two.

distractorRationale.b: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side. "Although..." is dependent, so the left side could never stand alone as a sentence.
distractorRationale.d: A full stop would leave the "Although" clause as a sentence fragment, and it would strand the main clause, whose "which is why" depends on the contrast the fragment was setting up.
distractorRationale.c: A colon must follow a complete clause and introduce an explanation, a list or an elaboration. Here the words before the blank form a dependent clause, and what follows is the sentence's own main clause rather than an elaboration of it.

accessibilityText: A sentence beginning with the word Although, about candle smoke absorbed by fresco plaster, with a blank after the words 'centuries of candle smoke' and before the main clause. Choose the punctuation that should follow the word smoke. Option A is smoke followed by a semicolon, option B is smoke followed by a comma, option C is smoke followed by a full stop, option D is smoke followed by a colon.

provenance.notes: Original item. The sentence was written for this bank; fresco conservation is described in general terms and no source text was adapted.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The sentence opens with a dependent 'Although' clause, which must be joined to the main clause ('the pigment ... survives') with a comma, so the answer is (a). (b), (c) and (d) each cut the 'Although' clause off as a fragment. A semicolon, colon or period needs an independent clause on both sides.

review.notes: Author solved and checked uniqueness: the leading 'Although' makes the first clause dependent, so the three marks that require an independent clause on the left all fail and only the comma joins.
